title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the leaflet to the poem

questions.prompt: A guide stops in the courtyard: "This is a one-hundred-year-old olive tree." Unpack the compound — which sentence says exactly the same thing?

options.text: The olive tree is one hundred years old.
The olive tree has one hundred years.
The olive tree is one hundred years olds.
The olive tree is aged of one hundred years.

questions.explanation: Once the compound leaves its place in front of the noun, it has to be unpacked, and English unpacks an age with the verb be: the tree is one hundred years old. Saying that it "has" one hundred years copies French straight into English and is the most frequent age mistake of the bac. The adjective old never takes an -s, since adjectives do not agree in English. And "aged of" is a translation too: we write aged one hundred, with no of.

questions.prompt: English puts the main stress on the FIRST word of a compound noun — a FILM director, a BOX office — while an ordinary adjective and its noun keep it on the noun. In which of these phrases does the main stress fall on the first word?
questions.explanation: A ticket office is one thing with one name, a compound noun in two words, so the stress moves forward onto TICKet — the same movement as in FILM director and BOX office. The three others are an adjective describing a noun, and there the noun keeps the stress: a crowded FOYer, a live CONcert, a free perFORmance. The difference is audible and it carries meaning: a BLACKbird is a species, a black BIRD is any bird of that colour.

questions.prompt: A brochure has to describe "a school that trains actors" in front of the noun. Which compound does it print?
questions.explanation: Here the school does the training, so the compound takes the -ing form and the noun that receives the action goes in front of it: an actor-training school, exactly like an elephant-training centre. The past participle would turn everything round — an actor-trained school would be a school trained by actors. The noun inside stays singular however many actors pass through, and reversing the two parts leaves a phrase that describes an actor rather than a school.

questions.prompt: A festival poster announces a "posthumous album" by a singer. What does the word tell you?

options.text: it was recorded before he was famous
it came out after his death
it brings together his greatest hits
it was released without his agreement

questions.explanation: Posthumous describes anything that happens after a person has died — a posthumous album, a posthumous prize, posthumous fame. It says when, not how: the songs may be old recordings or new mixes, and the singer's family may well have agreed to the release. Nor does the word promise a collection of hits; that is what a compilation is. Keep it beside the other words of praise from the same page: pioneering, single-handedly, stature and indisputably.

questions.prompt: Your poem has two quatrains. The first rhymes a b a b, and the second brings in four completely new rhyming sounds. How is the second stanza's scheme written?
questions.explanation: The letters name sounds, not positions, so a new sound always takes a new letter: the second stanza rhymes c d c d. Writing a b a b again would claim that its lines rhyme with the first stanza's lines, which is precisely what "completely new sounds" rules out, and b a b a would claim it even more strongly by reusing the same two sounds in the other order. As for a a b b, that is a real scheme — rhyming couplets — but it pairs line 1 with line 2, and the stanza described here alternates.

questions.prompt: The cinema prints its prices: "Adults £7.90 · Children aged 14 and under £4.95 · Under 3 free". Sami is 14 and brings his sister, who is two. What do the two of them pay altogether?
questions.explanation: Place each visitor in a category before you add anything. "Aged 14 and under" includes fourteen, so Sami pays the child price of £4.95; his sister is two, which falls under three, so she pays nothing — and £4.95 plus nothing is £4.95. Paying twice the child price forgets that free means free, £12.85 promotes Sami to the adult rate he has not reached, and £7.90 charges an adult who is not there. In a price list the boundary words — under, up to, and under, from — do as much work as the figures.
